en.title: The Glory and the Dream
en.author: William Manchester
en.subtitle: A Narrative History of America, 1932–1972 · 《光荣与梦想》
en.before: Before reading, twentieth-century U.S. history felt like a sequence of already named eras and events, each with a clear beginning and end. Looking backward made crisis, repair, and progress appear almost inevitable, and made growth itself feel like the normal condition of society.

shift.text: Manchester's continuous 1932–1972 narrative replaced a retrospective success story with the uncertainty of lived history. The central question shifted from why America became strong to how a society repeatedly facing crisis, conflict, error, and distrust could still keep operating and repairing itself.

en.after: The book made high-speed growth feel less like a permanent baseline and more like the climate of a particular era. It also changed the criterion for judging a society: not whether it avoids crisis, but whether conflict still leaves room for argument, correction, repair, and continued collective life.
en.return: Return to the book to keep asking what allows a society, after repeated episodes of disorder, to recover enough order to continue. The durable question is not why a country becomes powerful, but what remains unbroken when stability has to be rebuilt again and again.
